claims.text: The starting alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Conventionally cast or rapidly solidified CoCrFeNiTi can be obtained as a single-phase solid solution.
Simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
Simple-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi has high plasticity and machinability.
Chemical disorder in CoCrFeNiTi produces low lattice friction.
Low lattice friction permits relatively unimpeded dislocation glide.
Easy dislocation glide accounts for the alloy's lower hardness and strength.
Easy dislocation glide accounts for the alloy's ductility and machinability.
Annealing CoCrFeNiTi at 300–600 °C for a controlled time can induce nanoscale chemical ordering or precipitation without producing coarse secondary phases.
Fine precipitates can act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Short-range chemically ordered regions can act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy strength and hardness.
Smaller precipitates and their size and volume-fraction distribution can enhance precipitation strengthening.
Producing fine precipitates or chemical ordering in CoCrFeNiTi will increase yield and tensile or compressive strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Producing fine precipitates or chemical ordering in CoCrFeNiTi will increase Vickers hardness relative to the untreated alloy.
The strengthening treatment will moderately reduce ductility.
The heat-treated alloy will retain workable plasticity and machinability.
The proposed scope is limited to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi, 300–600 °C heat treatments, and mechanical testing from 25–600 °C.

contradictions.description: The prediction is conditional on successful formation of nanoscale ordering or precipitates, but the falsification rule treats failure to form those features as refutation of the mechanism. Failure of the intervention to create the mediator would not by itself falsify the mediator-to-strengthening hypothesis.
